title: Science teaching self-reflection | Read the goal through a piece of student work

qcReview.basis: The 4 English item texts and order match the corresponding factor in Kang et al. Appendix B, pp. 510–513. The original study used five frequency positions; methods §3.1 lists only endpoints 1 = rarely and 5 = always. The project preserves numeric 2–4 and the complete-response 1–5 factor mean. No study averages, norms or thresholds are used.

interpretations.headline: Read the goal through a piece of student work
interpretations.summary:
A curriculum statement asks learners to use evidence to explain a change, but the planned task only asks them to name the change. A quick look at a sample answer makes the difference visible. The teacher rewrites the task so students use a result to explain how they know.

The average reflects your own sense of how well you know the relevant science curriculum, the inquiry practices it calls for, and how you consider those goals in planning. It can help you choose a part of the curriculum to revisit. What you feel ready to teach and what a class can demonstrate are two sources of information you can consider together.

guidance.text: Choose one curriculum goal. Mark the science idea, the thinking or inquiry action students need, and what a convincing response might look like. Compare it with the task you usually set.
Check your reading with a colleague or an official curriculum example when the goal can reasonably be interpreted in more than one way.

limitations: Kang, N.-H., Kang, H., Maeng, S., Park, J., & Jeong, E. (2020). Teacher Competency in Competency-Focused Science Teaching in the South Korean Context: Teacher Self-Assessment Instrument Development and Application. Asia-Pacific Science Education, 6(2), 480–513. https://doi.org/10.1163/23641177-BJA10012 (CC BY 4.0, https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). The project separates each published factor and supplies its own instructions, complete-answer rule and feedback.

This score is the mean of 4 responses, from 1 (rarely) to 5 (always), and requires all 4 answers. It describes self-reported practices and may include judgments about your understanding or effectiveness. It contains no objective performance score, norm, or cross-factor total.

The original study used the full instrument with 210 South Korean primary and secondary science teachers. This research and self-reflection version uses the published English item wording. The project has not obtained the Korean administration form. Separate use of this factor and equivalence to a Chinese version have not been established.
report.disclaimer: For your own professional learning and research reflection as a science teacher. The result supports a conversation about practice and does not establish teaching quality, teacher eligibility, or student outcomes.
